title: Philosophy: Big Ideas · Episode 2
chapters: Philosophy's golden age in the Islamic world
Three ways to decide what's right
Descartes: I think, therefore I am

units.t: Philosophy: Big Ideas. Episode two.
In this episode: Philosophy's golden age in the Islamic world, Three ways to decide what's right, Descartes: I think, therefore I am and The Enlightenment.
Part one. Philosophy's golden age in the Islamic world.
Between Ancient Greece and the European Renaissance, some of the boldest philosophy on Earth was written in Arabic.
Meet the thinkers who preserved Aristotle, argued about cause and effect, and imagined a man floating in the air.
Translating the Greeks.
In the late 700s and 800s, under the Abbasid caliphs based in Baghdad, a remarkable translation movement got under way.
Scholars, many of them Christians fluent in Greek and Syriac, translated Aristotle, Plato's ideas as passed down by later writers, and Greek medicine, astronomy and mathematics into Arabic.
Wealthy patrons paid well.
Baghdad's House of Wisdom is often associated with the movement, although historians debate how far it was a formal academy rather than a palace library.
Much of this learning was scarcely read in Western Europe at the time.
It became part of a lively intellectual culture stretching from Central Asia to Spain.
Thinkers did not just preserve these texts; they argued with them.
The first philosophers.
Al-Kindi, working in Baghdad in the 800s, is often called 'the philosopher of the Arabs'.
He argued that truth should be welcomed whatever its source, even foreign peoples, and that philosophy and revelation pointed in the same direction.
A generation or two later, al-Farabi, who probably came from Central Asia, became so respected as an interpreter of Aristotle that he was called 'the Second Teacher'.
He wrote on logic, music and especially politics.
Inspired partly by Plato's Republic, he described a 'virtuous city' led by a wise ruler who would guide citizens towards true happiness.
His work shaped how later thinkers connected philosophy, religion and the good society.
Avicenna's floating man.
Ibn Sina, known in Europe as Avicenna, was born around 980 near Bukhara, in today's Uzbekistan.
By his own account he mastered most sciences by eighteen.
His Canon of Medicine served as a medical textbook in Europe for centuries.
In philosophy, he distinguished what a thing is, its essence, from the fact that it exists: you can understand a unicorn without knowing whether any exist.
He argued for a necessary being, whose essence includes existence, identified with God.
His best-known thought experiment imagines a person created in mid-air, blindfolded, limbs apart, with no sensations.
Would they know they exist?
Avicenna said yes, taking this to show the self is distinct from the body.
It resembles Descartes's argument six centuries later.
Critics question whether imagining yourself without a body shows you could exist without one.
Al-Ghazali and Averroes.
Not everyone welcomed the philosophers' confidence.
In the late 1000s, Abu Hamid al-Ghazali wrote The Incoherence of the Philosophers, attacking Avicenna and others.
His most striking argument concerned causation.
When cotton touches fire, it burns.
But we observe only that burning follows contact, never a necessary connection.
He concluded that God directly creates each event, usually in regular patterns, so miracles are possible.
Centuries later David Hume made a similar observation for very different reasons.
In the 1100s, in Córdoba, the judge and physician Ibn Rushd, or Averroes, replied with The Incoherence of the Incoherence.
He argued that religious law itself encouraged capable people to study nature through reason.
His commentaries on Aristotle became so influential in Latin translation that Thomas Aquinas called him simply 'the Commentator'.
A shared inheritance.
This was not only a Muslim story.
The Jewish philosopher Moses Maimonides, born in Córdoba and later working in Egypt, wrote his Guide for the Perplexed in Arabic, engaging closely with Aristotle and Islamic philosophy.
Christian scholars in Spain translated Arabic works into Latin, feeding the rise of medieval European universities.
Ibn Tufayl wrote a philosophical novel about a boy raised alone on an island who reasons his way to deep truths.
It may have been known in Europe by the time of Robinson Crusoe.
It is also a myth that Islamic philosophy ended in the 1100s.
It continued to flourish, especially in Persia, with thinkers such as Mulla Sadra in the 1600s.
These debates on reason, faith and the self belong to everyone's intellectual history.
The key idea: From the late 700s, scholars under the Abbasid caliphs translated Greek philosophy and science into Arabic, and argued with it.
Part two. Three ways to decide what's right.
Would you pull the lever?
Philosophy's three big approaches to right and wrong, and how they help with real decisions.
Judging by results.
Ethics, or moral philosophy, asks how we should live and act.
Most of the time our instincts work fine: don't steal, keep promises, help people in need.
But instincts can conflict, and some decisions in medicine, business, technology and our own lives are genuinely hard.
Three approaches dominate: consequentialism, deontology and virtue ethics.
Consequentialism says the right action has the best consequences.
Its most famous form, utilitarianism, was developed by Jeremy Bentham and John Stuart Mill: act to produce the greatest wellbeing for the greatest number.
It is practical and impartial, since everyone counts equally, and it underpins policy like cost-benefit analysis in health funding.
Australian philosopher Peter Singer is a leading modern advocate.
The trouble with results.
Imagine a surgeon with five patients who will die without organ transplants, and a healthy visitor whose organs could save them all.
Pure consequence-counting seems to say: sacrifice the visitor.
Almost everyone recoils.
The approach has other problems.
It demands that we predict consequences, which is often impossible, and it can seem to ignore justice, rights and promises.
Defenders respond that, in practice, respecting rights usually produces the best outcomes anyway.
Still, the surgeon case shows why many people feel that results cannot be the whole story.
Duties and rules.
Deontology, from the Greek for 'duty', says some actions are right or wrong in themselves, whatever the consequences.
Lying, killing innocent people and breaking promises are wrong even if they'd produce good results.
Immanuel Kant argued we should act only on principles we could want everyone to follow, and treat people as ends in themselves, never merely as means.
That explains why sacrificing the visitor is wrong: it uses him as a tool.
Human rights reflect this thinking.
Rules have problems too.
Kant argued you shouldn't lie even to a murderer asking where your friend is hiding, which strikes most people as absurd.
Duties can also conflict.
Many modern deontologists allow that duties can sometimes be outweighed, but deciding when is the hard part.
Becoming a good person.
Virtue ethics, going back to Aristotle in ancient Greece, shifts the question from 'What should I do?'
to 'What kind of person should I be?'
It focuses on developing good character traits, or virtues, like honesty, courage, compassion, fairness and wisdom.
Aristotle argued that virtues sit between extremes: courage lies between cowardice and recklessness, and generosity between stinginess and extravagance.
Good people develop practical wisdom, the ability to judge what each situation needs, through experience and habit.
Instead of a formula, virtue ethics offers a standard to grow towards.
The trolley and three lenses.
In the famous trolley problem, a runaway tram will kill five people unless you pull a lever to divert it onto a track where it will kill one.
Most people say pull it.
But if the only way to stop the tram is to push a large person off a bridge, most refuse, though the numbers are identical.
Our intuitions draw on both consequences and duties.
So don't pick one theory.
Try three lenses.
Consequences: who is affected, and how?
Duties: am I respecting rights and keeping commitments?
Character: what would a person I admire do?
Often all three agree.
When they don't, the tension shows what is at stake, which is where good judgement begins.
A quick test: would you be comfortable if the decision appeared on the front page?
The key idea: Consequentialism judges actions by their results, and utilitarianism aims for the greatest good for the greatest number.
Part three. Descartes: I think, therefore I am.
What if everything you believe is a dream, or a trick?
René Descartes set out to doubt everything he possibly could, and what was left became one of the most famous sentences ever written.
Doubting everything.
In the winter of 1619, a young Frenchman named René Descartes was stuck in Germany, serving with an army.
By his own account, he spent a day alone in a stove-heated room, thinking.
Despite an excellent education, he felt much of what he had learned was uncertain.
Admiring the step-by-step certainty of geometry, he resolved to clear away every belief that could be doubted and see what solid ground remained.
In his Meditations of 1641 he began with the senses.
A tower looks round from far away and square up close; a straight stick looks bent in water.
A source that has fooled you once is not safe to trust fully.
This was a tool for one quiet hour of reflection, not a way to live as a sceptic.
The dream and the demon.
Descartes then raised a stronger worry.
He had often dreamed he was sitting by the fire in his dressing gown when he was actually asleep in bed.
Is there any sure sign that separates waking life from a vivid dream?
If not, even the scene in front of him might be unreal.
Finally he imagined an evil demon, supremely powerful and cunning, devoting all its energy to deceiving him about everything, perhaps even simple sums.
Modern philosophers have updated the demon into a brain in a vat, fed false experiences by scientists, an idea that inspired films such as The Matrix.
The question is the same: can you prove this is not happening to you right now?
The one certainty.
Here Descartes found his foothold.
Suppose the demon deceives him about everything.
Still, to be deceived, he must exist.
To doubt, he must be thinking.
However far the doubt is pushed, it cannot reach the fact that there is a doubter.
In the Meditations he put it as 'I am, I exist', which must be true whenever he thinks it.
In his earlier Discourse on the Method of 1637, written in French, he used the form that became famous, usually rendered in Latin as cogito, ergo sum: I think, therefore I am.
The early Christian thinker Augustine had made a similar point more than a thousand years earlier, arguing that if he was mistaken, he must exist to be mistaken.
Rebuilding, and mind and body.
Knowing only that you exist is a lonely position.
Descartes argued that his idea of a perfect being could only come from a perfect God, who would not deceive him, so clear and distinct perceptions could be trusted.
Critics noted the Cartesian circle: he seems to use clear ideas to prove God, then God to guarantee clear ideas.
His method also led to dualism.
He could doubt having a body but not that he was thinking, so mind must be a different kind of thing from body.
From 1643 Princess Elisabeth of Bohemia pressed him: if the mind is not physical, how can it move an arm?
He suggested the pineal gland in the brain, an answer few found satisfying.
Most philosophers and scientists today reject his dualism.
Why he still matters.
Descartes died in Stockholm in 1650, not long after moving there at the invitation of Queen Christina of Sweden.
By starting from the individual mind and asking what it can know for certain, he put epistemology, the study of knowledge, at the centre of philosophy for centuries.
Later thinkers such as John Locke and David Hume answered him by stressing experience over pure reason.
He also helped shape modern science and gave us coordinate geometry, the familiar x and y axes, called Cartesian coordinates.
Even people who reject his conclusions use his method: when in doubt, slow down, question your assumptions and ask what you really have good reason to believe.
The key idea: Descartes set out to clear away every doubtful belief and rebuild knowledge on a foundation that could not be doubted.
Part four. The Enlightenment.
In the 1700s, thinkers argued that reason, not tradition or kings, should guide human life.
Their ideas built the modern world.
Dare to know.
In 1784 the German philosopher Immanuel Kant answered the question 'What is Enlightenment?'
with a motto borrowed from the Roman poet Horace: sapere aude, 'dare to know'.
He meant having the courage to use your own understanding without being guided by someone else.

Building on the Scientific Revolution, thinkers across Europe and its colonies argued that reason and evidence, not tradition or superstition, should guide how we understand the world and organise society.
Isaac Newton's Principia, 1687, showed a few laws explaining both falling apples and orbiting planets.
If nature followed rational laws, why not society too?
The movement is usually dated from the late 1600s to around 1800.
Spreading the ideas.
Ideas spread through coffee houses, scientific societies, Parisian salons often hosted by women, and a booming trade in books.
The great project was the Encyclopédie, edited by Denis Diderot and Jean le Rond d'Alembert and published from 1751.
It aimed to gather all human knowledge, including practical trades, and French authorities repeatedly banned it.
Voltaire, 1694 to 1778, used wit and satire to attack intolerance and censorship.
His novel Candide, 1759, mocks the idea that we live in the best of all possible worlds.
He was jailed in the Bastille, spent years in exile, and in 1765 helped clear Jean Calas, a Protestant wrongly executed in 1762.
The famous line 'I disapprove of what you say, but I will defend to the death your right to say it' wasn't his.
His biographer Evelyn Beatrice Hall wrote it in 1906.
Rights and consent.
The English philosopher John Locke, 1632 to 1704, argued that people are born with natural rights, including life, liberty and property, and that governments exist to protect them.
Government rests on the consent of the governed.
If it violates those rights, people may replace it.
In his Essay Concerning Human Understanding, 1689, he argued that the mind at birth is like a blank slate, shaped by experience rather than inborn ideas.
He also made an influential case for religious toleration.
His ideas deeply influenced the American Declaration of Independence, with its 'life, liberty and the pursuit of happiness', and later democratic constitutions.
Dividing power.
In The Spirit of the Laws, 1748, Montesquieu argued liberty is safest when power is divided: one body makes laws, another carries them out, and an independent judiciary interprets them.
Each checks the others, so no one becomes all-powerful.
This separation of powers became central to the US Constitution.
Australia's Constitution also separates legislative, executive and judicial power, and the High Court guarded judicial independence in the 1956 Boilermakers' case.
Jean-Jacques Rousseau opened The Social Contract, 1762, with: 'Man is born free, and everywhere he is in chains.'
He argued legitimate authority comes from the collective will of the people, not kings or force.
Critics note his claim that dissenters can be 'forced to be free' could justify authoritarianism.
Mary Wollstonecraft's Vindication of the Rights of Woman, 1792, extended these arguments to women.
Science, legacy, blind spots.
The Scottish Enlightenment produced David Hume, Adam Smith, The Wealth of Nations, 1776, and James Hutton, who argued the Earth was far older than most believed.
Enlightenment science reached Australia too: James Cook's voyage, backed by the Royal Society, observed the 1769 transit of Venus from Tahiti, then charted the east coast in 1770.
Joseph Banks collected thousands of plant specimens.
Free speech, tolerance, democracy and equal rights are Enlightenment legacies, running through the 1948 Universal Declaration of Human Rights.
But many thinkers accepted slavery, colonialism or the exclusion of women.
British colonisation of Australia began in 1788, with devastating effects on Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples.
Many argue the answer is to apply Enlightenment principles more consistently, not abandon them.
The key idea: The Enlightenment championed reason, evidence and individual rights over tradition and unquestioned authority.
Quick recall. Answer out loud, or just in your head.
Question one. What did the Abbasid-era translators help achieve?
Answer. Greek learning was absorbed into Arabic thought and debated.
Question two. What does utilitarianism say makes an action right?
Answer. It brings the greatest wellbeing overall.
Question three. What was Descartes trying to do with his method of doubt?
Answer. Clear away doubtful beliefs to find a certain foundation.
Question four. What did Kant mean by 'dare to know'?
Answer. Using your own understanding with courage.
That's the end of this episode. The questions are waiting in your review, so you can lock in what you heard.
